## Today

**Today's view: a role-play. We are the trial statistician of one randomized
trial with a survival endpoint, from protocol to submission.**

* Plan the trial: protocol, estimand, SAP, group sequential design, sample size
* Collect the data: CRF, raw data, SDTM, ADaM
* Report the results: TFL shells, tables and figures, the R packages behind them
* Monitor the trial: interim analysis, p-values, conditional power
* Submit the package: datasets, metadata, reviewer's guides

Every number on these slides comes from the code in **`lab/`**. You can run
the code on Posit Cloud, on your own computer, or with Claude.

::: notes
This lecture is a role-play, not a methods lecture. We act as the trial
statistician and use the survival methods from this course on one trial. Ask
students to open the repository now so they can follow along.
:::

## Glossary

Clinical trials use many acronyms. The slides spell out each acronym at first
use. Full list: `lab/docs/00_glossary.md`.

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
* **SAP**: Statistical Analysis Plan
* **CRF**: Case Report Form; **EDC**: Electronic Data Capture
* **CDISC**: Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium
* **SDTM**: Study Data Tabulation Model (collected data)
* **ADaM**: Analysis Data Model (analysis-ready data)
* **TFL**: Tables, Figures and Listings
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
* **PFS**: Progression-Free Survival; **OS**: Overall Survival
* **ORR**: Objective Response Rate
* **TEAE**: Treatment-Emergent Adverse Event
* **DMC**: Data Monitoring Committee
* **IA**: Interim Analysis
* **CP**: Conditional Power
:::
::::

# Part 1 · The map of a trial {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Who does what, and our example trial

## The statistician's role in a trial

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box lead"><b>Protocol</b>objectives, endpoints, sample size</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>SAP + shells</b>all analyses planned in advance</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>CRF / EDC</b>collect what the SAP needs</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Raw data</b>EDC export + vendor files</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>SDTM</b>standard format for collected data</div>
</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box review"><b>ADaM</b>datasets ready for analysis (the statistician writes the specifications)</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>TFLs</b>tables, figures, listings</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>Clinical study report</b>results and interpretation</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Submission</b>datasets and reports for the regulator</div>
</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box dashed"><b>Interim analysis</b>same ADaM + TFL programs on a data cut &rarr; Data Monitoring Committee &rarr; continue / stop</div>
</div>
```

[<span class="legend-lead"></span> statistician leads &nbsp;&nbsp; <span class="legend-review"></span> statistician specifies and reviews]{.small}

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The statistician is responsible for**: design, sample size, SAP, shells,
ADaM specifications, interim plan, interpretation.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The statistician works with**: clinicians (endpoints), data managers (CRF,
data cleaning), statistical programmers (SDTM, ADaM and TFL code), regulatory
affairs (submission).
:::
::::

::: notes
The interim analysis can change the course of the trial; this possibility is
the reason for group sequential designs. Programmers write most of the code,
but the statistician decides what the code must do and approves the results.
:::

## Our example trial: CDISCPILOT01

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
* Data from **pharmaverse** (`pharmaversesdtm`, `pharmaverseadam`):
  the CDISC SDTM/ADaM pilot study, xanomeline patch vs placebo
* Standard CDISC structure: `r nrow(adsl)` patients screened,
  `r sum(adsl$ITTFL == "Y")` randomized 1:1:1
* Plus **synthetic RECIST 1.1 tumour assessments** (`rs_onco`)
* In this lecture, the study is an oncology trial:
  * **Primary**: PFS, High Dose vs Placebo
  * **Secondary**: PFS Low Dose vs Placebo, ORR, OS
  * **Safety**: adverse events, laboratory tests
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
adsl |>
  dplyr::mutate(Arm = factor(TRT01P, levels = c(ARM_LEVELS, "Screen Failure"))) |>
  dplyr::count(Arm, name = "Patients") |>
  tab(20)
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
All data are synthetic test data from pharmaverse. We use no real patient data.
:::

# Part 2 · Planning {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Protocol, estimand, SAP, group sequential design, sample size

::: notes
Target: finish Part 2 by minute 30. Every later step carries out a decision made here.
:::

## Protocol: the parts the statistician writes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
| | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| Primary | **PFS**: randomization to first progression (RECIST 1.1, investigator) or death |
| Key secondary | PFS, Low Dose vs Placebo |
| Secondary | **ORR**: best overall response CR or PR |
| Secondary | **OS**: randomization to death |
| Safety | TEAEs (MedDRA), labs (CTCAE grades) |

[RECIST: Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; CR/PR: complete/partial response; MedDRA: Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities; CTCAE: Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events]{.tiny .muted}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Also written by the statistician**

* Hypotheses and alpha: H0: HR = 1 vs H1: HR < 1, one-sided 2.5%
* Design: 1:1:1, event-driven, one interim analysis
* Sample size and assumptions
* Analysis populations and methods (summary)
* Multiplicity strategy
* Interim analysis and DMC charter

Full text: `lab/docs/01_protocol_synopsis.md`
:::
::::

## The estimand (ICH E9(R1))

An estimand defines **what** we estimate, before we decide **how** to estimate. ICH: International Council for Harmonisation.

| Attribute | PFS, High Dose vs Placebo |
|---|---|
| Population | All randomized patients (intention-to-treat, ITT) |
| Treatment | High Dose vs placebo, added to best supportive care |
| Variable | Time to progression (RECIST 1.1) or death |
| Intercurrent events | Stops treatment early: *treatment policy* (keep scanning) · Death: part of the endpoint (*composite*) · New anticancer therapy: *hypothetical* (censor before the new therapy) |
| Summary measure | Hazard ratio (Cox model), tested by log-rank |

::: {.takeaway}
Censoring rules are not programming details: the rules define how the estimand
handles intercurrent events. Write the rules in the SAP, then program the rules
exactly as written.
:::

## SAP: decide everything before unblinding

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Definitions**

* Analysis sets and the ADSL flag for each
* Study day, baseline, visit windows
* Treatment-emergent adverse event window
* Partial date imputation (ADaM only, never SDTM)
* Endpoint derivations and **censoring rules**

**Methods**

* Test, model, stratification factors
* Confidence interval (CI) method (for example exact or log-log), handling of ties
* Sensitivity and subgroup analyses
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Error control**

* Multiplicity strategy across endpoints and doses
* Interim analyses: timing, boundaries, futility

**Outputs**

* TFL shells: every table, figure and listing, with titles, populations and footnotes

**Process**

* Final version before database lock (DBL) and before anyone sees unblinded data

Excerpt: `lab/docs/02_sap.md`
:::
::::

## Analysis sets become ADSL flags

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| Set | Definition | Flag |
|---|---|---|
| ITT | All randomized, **as randomized** | `ITTFL`, `TRT01P` |
| Safety | All dosed, **as treated** | `SAFFL`, `TRT01A` |

[ADSL: subject-level analysis dataset, one row per patient]{.small .muted}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
adsl |>
  dplyr::filter(ITTFL == "Y") |>
  dplyr::count(`Randomized (TRT01P)` = TRT01P, `Received (TRT01A)` = TRT01A, name = "Patients") |>
  tab(20)
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
`r sum(adsl$TRT01P == "Xanomeline High Dose" & adsl$TRT01A == "Xanomeline Low Dose")`
patients randomized to High Dose stopped treatment during the first 54 mg period
and never received 81 mg. These patients count as High Dose for efficacy and as
Low Dose for safety.
:::

## PFS censoring rules (SAP section 6.1)

| Situation | Date | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Progression documented (RECIST 1.1) | Date of the first scan showing progression | **Event** |
| Death before progression | Date of death | **Event** |
| No progression, no death | Last adequate tumour assessment | Censored |
| No post-baseline assessment, no death | Randomization | Censored |
| New anticancer therapy before progression | Last adequate assessment before the new therapy | Censored |
| Event after two or more missed scans | Last adequate assessment before the gap | Censored (sensitivity) |

[Adapted from US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance *Clinical Trial Endpoints for the Approval of Cancer Drugs and Biologics* (2018). Part 3 turns this table into code.]{.small .muted}

## Why a group sequential design?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
* Look at the data **before** the planned end: stop early for efficacy, or for futility
* Each look adds a chance of a false positive result: split the one-sided 2.5% alpha across the looks
* **Alpha spending function** (Lan-DeMets, O'Brien-Fleming type), with information fraction $t$ = events observed / events planned:

$$
\alpha(t) = 2\left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{t}}\right)\right]
$$

* The function spends very little alpha early, so the final boundary stays close to 1.96
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_boundary
```
:::
::::

## The design in {rpact}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r design-gsd, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
boundary_tbl |>
  dplyr::select(-`Months from first randomization`, -`Futility boundary (Z)`) |>
  tab(16)
```

* Stopping for efficacy at the interim needs p < `r signif(design$stageLevels[1], 2)` (an observed HR of about 0.5 or lower)
* The final boundary is only slightly larger than for a single test: `r round(design$criticalValues[2], 3)` vs 1.960
* The futility rule is **non-binding**: continuing after the rule is met does not increase alpha
:::
::::

## Sample size for survival: power comes from events

Schoenfeld's formula (1:1 allocation, log-rank test):

$$
d = \frac{4\,(z_{1-\alpha} + z_{1-\beta})^2}{(\log \mathrm{HR})^2}
= \frac{4\,(1.960 + 0.842)^2}{(\log 0.6)^2} \approx `r round(events_fixed, 1)`
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r design-schoenfeld, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
* Fixed design: `r round(events_fixed, 1)` events
* × inflation factor `r round(inflation, 4)` for the interim
* = `r round(events_gsd, 1)` → **`r target_events` events**; interim at **`r ia_events`**

::: {.takeaway}
The number of patients only changes **how long** the trial needs to observe the events.
:::
:::
::::

## From events to patients

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r design-samplesize, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
Assumptions: placebo median PFS `r DESIGN$median_control` months (placebo arms of
refractory colorectal cancer trials such as CORRECT and RECOURSE), HR 0.60, 24-month
enrollment period, 3-month minimum follow-up, 25% dropout by month 3.

* **`r round(ss$maxNumberOfSubjects, 1)` → `r 2 * n_per_arm` patients** (`r n_per_arm` per arm) for the primary comparison
* With the Low Dose arm: **`r 3 * n_per_arm`** planned; the study randomized `r sum(adsl$ITTFL == "Y")`
* Expected timing: interim at month `r round(ss$analysisTime[1, 1], 1)`, final at month `r round(ss$analysisTime[2, 1], 1)`
:::
::::

## How sensitive is the plan to the assumptions?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
sens_tbl |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_style(gt::cell_fill(color = "#EEF5FB"), gt::cells_body(rows = `Assumed HR` == 0.6)) |>
  slide_gt(20)
```
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
* Events needed grow like $1 / (\log \mathrm{HR})^2$: HR 0.70 needs twice the events of HR 0.60
* The HR is the most important and least certain assumption: justify the HR with data from earlier trials
* Proportional hazards is also an assumption. A delayed treatment effect (common with immunotherapy) reduces power.
* In an event-driven trial, monitor the **pooled, blinded** event count and update the predicted analysis dates
:::
::::

# Part 3 · Data standards {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

CRF → raw data → SDTM → ADaM

::: notes
Target: finish Part 3 by minute 50. Students rarely see raw data; show the formats and the QC story.
:::

## Collect only what the SAP needs

| SAP needs | Source | Raw file in `lab/data/raw/` | SDTM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Randomized arm and date | IRT vendor transfer | `irt.csv` | DM.ARM, DS |
| Age, sex, race | Demographics CRF | `dm.csv` | DM |
| First / last dose, dose received | Exposure CRF | `ex.csv` | EX, DM |
| Progression | Tumour response CRF | `rs.csv` | RS |
| Death, end of study | End of Study CRF | `ds.csv` | DS |
| Adverse events | Adverse event CRF + MedDRA coding | `ae.csv` | AE |
| Concomitant medications | Concomitant medication CRF + WHODrug coding | `cm.csv` | CM |
| Laboratory values | Central lab transfer | `lb.csv.gz` | LB |

[IRT: Interactive Response Technology (randomization system); CM: concomitant medications; WHODrug: World Health Organization Drug Dictionary]{.small .muted}

## The annotated CRF: Adverse Event page

| CRF question | CRF field (CDASH) | Raw value | SDTM variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adverse event term | `AETERM` | APPLICATION SITE ERYTHEMA | `AETERM` |
| Start date | `AESTDAT` | 03 JAN 2014 · UN JAN 2014 | `AESTDTC` = "2014-01-03" · "2014-01" |
| Severity | `AESEV` | Mild / Moderate / Severe | `AESEV` = MILD / MODERATE / SEVERE |
| Serious? | `AESER` | Yes / No | `AESER` = Y / N |
| Relationship to study drug | `AEREL` | None / Remote / Possible / Probable | `AEREL` |
| (coding team) | `AETERM_PT`, `AETERM_SOC` | APPLICATION SITE ERYTHEMA | `AEDECOD`, `AEBODSYS` |
| (derived) | | | `AESEQ`, `AESTDY` |

[CDASH: Clinical Data Acquisition Standards Harmonization, a standard for CRF field names that map to SDTM. PT: preferred term; SOC: system organ class.]{.small .muted}

## Example of raw data

```{r}
raw_ae <- read_raw("ae")
raw_ae |>
  dplyr::filter(SUBJECT %in% c("701-1015", "701-1023")) |>
  dplyr::select(SUBJECT, AETERM, AESTDAT, AEENDAT, AEONGO, AESEV, AESER, AEREL, AETERM_PT) |>
  head(7) |>
  tab(16)
```

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**EDC**: `"03 JAN 2014"`, unknown day `"UN JAN 2014"`, text pick-lists
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**IRT vendor**: date "`r irt_date_example`"
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Lab vendor**: date "`r lb_example$COLL_DATE`", time "`r lb_example$COLL_TIME`", units in two systems
:::
::::

## How we made the raw data

pharmaverse provides SDTM data only. The lab rebuilds raw data from SDTM
(**reverse engineering**): the code undoes the derivations that the SDTMIG
(SDTM Implementation Guide) asks a sponsor to do.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
1. Remove derived variables: `--SEQ`, `--DY`, `USUBJID`, `AGE`, reference dates
2. ISO 8601 dates → CRF text
3. Controlled terminology → CRF display text
4. Keep dictionary codes as "coding" columns
5. Reshape findings data into the layout of CRF and vendor files
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r raw-date-helpers, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::::

## SDTM: a short overview

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**One dataset per domain**, grouped in classes

* Special purpose: **DM** (demographics)
* Interventions: **EX** (exposure), **CM** (medications)
* Events: **AE** (adverse events), **DS** (disposition)
* Findings: **LB** (labs), **VS** (vitals), **RS** / **TU** / **TR** (tumour response, identification, results)
* Trial design: TA, TV, TS ...
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Common conventions**

* `USUBJID`: unique across all studies of the sponsor
* Dates in ISO 8601 (`--DTC`), partial dates stay partial
* Study day `--DY`: **no day 0**
* `--SEQ`: unique record number within patient
* Controlled terminology (CT): `SEX` is `"F"` or `"M"`
* Non-standard variables go to SUPPQUAL (supplemental qualifiers), e.g. `SUPPDM`
:::
::::

## Quality control (QC): compare with an independent version

```{r}
qc_summary |>
  tab(22)
```

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**DM `RFENDTC`, patient 01-710-1083.** The reference data use the date of the
end-of-study page. Our rule uses the date of the event (death). This difference
is a **specification ambiguity**: fix the specification, not only the code.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**AE `AESTDY`, patient 01-716-1063.** The adverse event starts on the first-dose
date, so the study day is 1. The reference data say 366. This difference is an
**error in the reference data**.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Regulated outputs are checked by independent double programming: two
programmers, one specification, then a comparison with {diffdf} or SAS PROC COMPARE.
:::

## ADaM: ready for analysis and traceable

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Principles (ADaM Implementation Guide, ADaMIG)**

* Ready for analysis: one procedure call gives the result
* Traceable: every value can be traced back to SDTM
* Documented by metadata (define.xml)

**Structures**

* **ADSL**: one row per patient
* **BDS** (Basic Data Structure): one row per patient × parameter × time point. ADLB, ADRS, **ADTTE**
* **OCCDS** (Occurrence Data Structure): ADAE, ADCM
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
| SDTM sources | ADaM dataset | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| DM, DS, VS, SUPPDM | **ADSL** | one row per patient |
| RS + ADSL | **ADRS** | BDS (response by visit, best overall response, progression) |
| ADSL + ADRS | **ADTTE** | BDS (PFS, OS) |
| AE + ADSL | **ADAE** | OCCDS |
| CM + ADSL | **ADCM** | OCCDS |
| LB + ADSL | **ADLB** | BDS (with CTCAE grades) |

[Built with {admiral} (pharmaverse): one function per derivation rule.]{.small .muted}
:::
::::

## ADSL: add the variables our SAP needs {.code-small}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r adsl-derive, opts.label = "code"}
```

adsl_check |>

## ADTTE: one row per patient per parameter

```{r}
adtte |>
  dplyr::filter(USUBJID %in% c("01-701-1015", "01-701-1023", "01-701-1028")) |>
  dplyr::select(USUBJID, PARAMCD, STARTDT, ADT, AVAL, CNSR, EVNTDESC, SRCDOM, SRCVAR, SRCSEQ) |>
  tab(18)
```

* `AVAL` = `ADT` − `STARTDT` + 1 (days); `CNSR` = 0 event, 1 censored
* `SRCDOM` / `SRCVAR` / `SRCSEQ`: **traceability**, the source record of the date

Shells, software, baseline, efficacy, safety

## TFL shells are part of the SAP

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Table 14.2.1** Progression-free survival (ITT set)

| | Placebo (N=xx) | Low (N=xx) | High (N=xx) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Events, n (%) | xx (xx.x) | xx (xx.x) | xx (xx.x) |
| Censored, n (%) | xx (xx.x) | xx (xx.x) | xx (xx.x) |
| Median, months (95% CI) [a] | x.x (x.x, x.x) | ... | ... |
| HR vs placebo (95% CI) [b] | Reference | x.xx (...) | x.xx (...) |
| One-sided p (log-rank) | | x.xxx | x.xxx |

[[a] Kaplan-Meier, Brookmeyer-Crowley CI (log-log). [b] Cox model.]{.tiny}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
* Written **before** any data exist and agreed by the statistician, clinicians and programmers
* Shells fix the numbering (ICH E3: 14.1 baseline, 14.2 efficacy, 14.3 safety), titles, population, rows, statistics, decimals and footnotes
* Programmers write code to match the shell; QC compares the output with the shell
* All shells: `lab/docs/04_tfl_shells.md`
:::
::::

## Software for each step

| Step | R packages used here | Other common tools |
|---|---|---|
| Design, sample size | **rpact** | gsDesign, East (commercial), SAS PROC SEQDESIGN |
| Raw → SDTM | dplyr (by hand) | **sdtm.oak** (pharmaverse), SAS |
| SDTM → ADaM | **admiral**, admiralonco, metatools | SAS macros |
| Survival analysis | **survival**, ggsurvfit | SAS PROC LIFETEST / PHREG |
| Tables | **gtsummary** (+ cards), gt | rtables + tern, Tplyr, r2rtf |
| Interim data cut | admiral functions with a cut-off date | **datacutr** (pharmaverse) |
| Submission files | **xportr** | metacore, SAS |
| QC | **diffdf** | SAS PROC COMPARE |
| Reproducibility | **renv**, git | containers |

## Why the curves have large steps

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
* Progression is only **seen at scheduled scans** (weeks 6, 12, 18, 24)
* The true progression time is somewhere between two scans: **interval-censored**
* Many tied event times at each scan
* If one arm has later or fewer scans, PFS is biased: use the same scan schedule in every arm
* Sensitivity analysis: interval-censored methods (for example `icenReg`), or a midpoint imputation
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
pfs |>
  dplyr::filter(CNSR == 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Week = round(AVAL / 7)) |>
  dplyr::count(`Study week of progression` = cut(Week, c(0, 4, 8, 10, 14, 20, 30),
                                                labels = c("0-4", "5-8", "9-10", "11-14", "15-20", "21-30"))) |>
  tab(20)
```
:::
::::

## The log-rank test, step by step

$$
Z = \frac{\sum_j \left(O_{1j} - E_{1j}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum_j V_{1j}}},\qquad
E_{1j} = d_j \frac{n_{1j}}{n_j},\qquad
V_{1j} = d_j \frac{n_{1j}\, n_{0j}\,(n_j - d_j)}{n_j^2\,(n_j - 1)}
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
logrank_parts |>
  tab(20)
```
:::
::::

Variance $V$ = `r round(logrank_var, 2)`, so
$Z = (E - O)/\sqrt{V}$ for High Dose = `r sprintf("%.1f", lr$exp[2] - lr$obs[2])` / `r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(logrank_var))`
= **`r sprintf("%.3f", pfs_hi$z)`**, one-sided p = **`r fmt_p(pfs_hi$p_one_sided)`**.

## Same data, different software defaults

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Output
```{r}
defaults_tbl |>
  tab(20)
```

::: {.takeaway}
The methods for ties and confidence intervals change the numbers. The SAP must
name the method (for example "Efron ties; Brookmeyer-Crowley CI with log-log
transformation"). Double programming in R and SAS matches only when both
programs use the same method.
:::
### Code
```{r eff-software-defaults, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::

## What can we claim? Multiplicity

```{r}
hier_tbl |>
  tab(20)
```

* The final boundary is recomputed with the **actual** information:
  `r ia_events_obs` events at the interim, `r pfs_hi$events` at the final → Z ≥ `r sprintf("%.3f", z_final)`
* The primary hypothesis is not rejected (HR `r sprintf("%.2f", pfs_hi$hr)`): testing stops, and all later results are **descriptive**
* Nominal p-values for later endpoints can be shown, but these p-values support no claim

## TFL production in practice

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Before the data arrive**

* Shells approved together with the SAP
* ADaM specifications (one row per variable, with derivation)
* Programs written and run on **blinded** or dummy-treatment data ("dry runs")

**Checks**

* Independent double programming of every key output
* N in column headers = analysis set size
* Footnotes state population, method, and data cut
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Reproducibility**

* Version control (git) for programs and specifications
* Locked package versions (`renv.lock`)
* One command reruns everything (`lab/run_all.R`)

**Statistician's review**

* Does each number answer the SAP question?
* Are the denominators right?
* Do numbers agree across tables (events in 14.2.1 vs ADTTE vs IA report)?
:::
::::

# Part 5 · Interim analysis {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Boundaries, p-values, conditional power, the DMC report

::: notes
Target: finish Part 5 by minute 82. Ask the room for a recommendation before showing the final result.
:::

## Steps of an interim analysis

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box review"><b>Track events</b>blinded, pooled across arms</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Cut-off date</b>date of the 61st event</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Clean data</b>up to the cut-off date</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>Re-run</b>the same ADaM and TFL programs on the cut data</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>Independent statistician</b>unblinded closed report</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>DMC</b>closed session, recommendation</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Sponsor</b>receives only the recommendation: continue / modify / stop</div>
</div>
```
* The sponsor's study team stays **blinded**: a separate, independent team does the unblinded work
* Open session: pooled data and trial conduct. Closed session: efficacy and safety by arm.

## The data cut in code: one program for every cut

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r adam-datacut, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r adtte-interim, opts.label = "code"}
```

Data cut-off date: **`r format(ia_dco)`**, `r ia$events` events in High Dose + Placebo.
:::
::::

## Interim result and the boundary

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_ia_boundary
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
* Information fraction `r ia$events` / `r target_events` = `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * info_frac)`: Lan-DeMets spending computes the boundary **at the actual fraction**
* HR `r sprintf("%.2f (95%% CI %.2f, %.2f)", ia$hr, ia$hr_lower, ia$hr_upper)`
* Z = `r sprintf("%.3f", ia$z)`, one-sided p = `r fmt_p(ia$p_one_sided)`
* Efficacy needs Z ≥ `r sprintf("%.3f", z_eff_ia)` (p ≤ `r sprintf("%.4f", p_eff_ia)`): **not crossed**
* Futility guideline Z < 0: **not met**
:::
::::

## Conditional power {.code-small}

$$
\mathrm{CP}(\theta) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{c_K \sqrt{I_K} - Z_k \sqrt{I_k} - \theta\,(I_K - I_k)}{\sqrt{I_K - I_k}}\right),
\qquad I \approx \frac{\text{events}}{4},\quad \theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r ia-conditional-power, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
cp_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(theta = round(theta, 3), `Conditional power` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * `Conditional power`)) |>
  tab(20)
```

{rpact} `getAnalysisResults()` gives `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cp_rpact_design)` under the design HR, the same result.

::: {.takeaway}
CP depends on the assumed effect. CP under the design HR is the most
optimistic number in the report. Always show CP under the current trend too.
:::
:::
::::

## Table IA.1 The DMC closed report (primary endpoint)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
slide_gt(t_ia_1, 18)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**What would you recommend?**

* The pre-specified rule (Z < 0) says: continue
* CP under the current trend is `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cp_tbl[["Conditional power"]][2])`
* The final analysis gave HR `r sprintf("%.2f", pfs_hi$hr)`, p = `r fmt_p(pfs_hi$p_one_sided)`: the trial did not succeed

A futility rule based on conditional power (for example CP < 10% under the
current trend) would have stopped the trial at the interim. The choice of rule
is a design decision: check the operating characteristics of the rule first.
:::
::::

# Part 6 · Deliverables and submission {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Deliverables during the trial, datasets, metadata, reviewer's guides

::: notes
Target: wrap up by minute 90, leave time for questions.
:::

## Submission is not the only deliverable

| Deliverable | When | Receiver | The statistician's work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interim analysis | At the planned number of events | DMC | Boundaries, conditional power, closed report (Part 5) |
| Safety reviews | Every few months, at each DMC or SRC meeting | DMC; Safety Review Committee (SRC) | Safety tables by arm, listings of deaths and serious adverse events |
| DSUR | Every year, for each drug in development | Regulators | Exposure and cumulative safety summaries |
| Ad-hoc requests | Any time, often with a short deadline | Regulators, DMC, medical team, publications | New tables, figures or analyses outside the SAP |
| CSR and submission | After database lock | Regulators | Final TFLs, datasets, metadata, reviewer's guides |

[DSUR: Development Safety Update Report (ICH E2F). CSR: Clinical Study Report.]{.small .muted}

::: {.takeaway}
One set of ADaM datasets and TFL programs serves all these deliverables: build
the programs once, then run the programs on each new data cut.
:::

## What the FDA receives

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
cat(ectd_tree)
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
* **XPT**: SAS transport files, version 5 (names ≤ 8 characters, labels ≤ 40)
* **define.xml**: metadata for every dataset, variable, code list and derivation
* **aCRF**: annotated CRF
* **cSDRG / ADRG**: Clinical Study Data Reviewer's Guide (SDTM) / Analysis Data Reviewer's Guide (ADaM)
* Programs for the primary and key secondary results
* Conformance checks (Pinnacle 21) with explanations

[eCTD: electronic Common Technical Document; module 5 holds clinical study reports and data.]{.small .muted}
:::
::::

## Metadata-driven XPT files with {xportr}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r sub-xportr, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
xpt_check |>
  head(12) |>
  tab(18)
```
:::
::::

## R in regulatory submissions

* The FDA does not require any specific software (Statistical Software Clarifying Statement, 2015). The FDA requires work that is documented and reproducible.
* The R Consortium submission pilots sent the FDA TFLs, a Shiny app and ADaM datasets, all built in R (github.com/RConsortium/submissions-wg)
* What reviewers need from an R submission:
  * package versions (`renv.lock`, `sessionInfo()`) and installation steps
  * programs that run on the submitted datasets and reproduce the numbers in the CSR
  * an ADRG that explains these items
* Many companies now use both R and SAS; double programming in two languages is common

## Five key messages {.larger}

1. **Write the SAP like code.** Every rule must have only one meaning; QC finds the gaps (`RFENDTC`).
2. **Power comes from events.** Design, predict and monitor events, not patients.
3. **Traceability.** CRF field → raw → SDTM → ADaM → the number in the table.
4. **An interim analysis reuses the final programs on a data cut**, and the boundaries use the actual information.
5. **Conditional power depends on the assumed effect.** Report CP under the design effect and under the current trend.
